guidance: This result does not establish food safety. Follow a current tested process, product directions, and authoritative food-safety guidance.
method: The plan runs backwards from the fermenter, because the batch volume in the fermenter is the number the brewer is trying to hit. The wort needed at flameout, chilled, is the batch plus the kettle loss; hot, it is that volume divided by 0.96, because wort contracts about 4 percent as it cools from boiling to pitching temperature (water is 0.9584 kg/L at 100 C against 0.9982 kg/L at 20 C). Adding the boil-off, the rate in litres per hour times the boil length in hours, gives the pre-boil volume. The grain holds its absorption rate times the grain bill, and adding that gives the total water to heat. Strike water is the grain bill times the mash thickness, and sparge water is the remainder of the total: cold = batch + kettle loss; hot = cold / 0.96; pre-boil = hot + boil-off x hours; absorbed = grain x absorption; total = pre-boil + absorbed; strike = grain x thickness; sparge = total - strike. Units are metric (litres, kilograms) or US customary (US gallons, pounds); 1 US gallon is 3.785411784 L, 1 pound is 0.45359237 kg, and 1 qt/lb is 2.086351 L/kg through 1 qt = 0.946352946 L. The absorption default of 1 L/kg sits near the middle of the 0.8-1.1 L/kg that homebrewing guides quote for a drained mash (0.1-0.125 gal/lb); it is equipment data, so the page takes it as an input rather than asserting a constant. Accepted ranges are 1-2,000 L batch, 0.1-500 kg grain, 1-10 L/kg mash thickness, 1-300 minutes boil, 0.1-50 L/h boil-off, 0-100 L kettle loss and 0.3-2 L/kg absorption, each with field-specific messages for blanks, malformed or out-of-range values. If the chosen mash thickness needs more water than the whole batch contains, the page refuses rather than printing a negative sparge: it names the thickness and the batch volume as the two numbers to change. The page plans volumes only. It does not estimate gravity, brewhouse efficiency, mash pH, hop absorption or fermentation, it leaves mash-tun dead space to be folded into the kettle loss, and it makes no food-safety claim.

sources.title: Brewers Association, All-Grain: Batch Sparging: strike water is grain weight x water-to-grain ratio, one pound of grain holds 0.1-0.125 gallons, pre-boil volume is batch volume + boil-off rate x boil duration, and sparge water makes up the difference
Palmer, J., How to Brew, Chapter 17: Sparging: mash and sparge water volumes, water retention of the grain bed, and the practice of sizing the sparge as the remainder of the pre-boil volume
Properties of water: density 958.4 kg/m3 at 100 C and 998.2 kg/m3 at 20 C, the roughly 4 percent contraction on cooling from the boil
